intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, gives you something to remember or warns where people slip. Work the examples in pencil, answer the recall questions before you check, and add your own marks beside mine.

sections.title: Why education policy matters
sections.big_idea: Access is largely won, so ask four questions of every scheme: access, **learning**, equity and money.
in_plain_words: Education policy is the set of public choices on who goes to school, for how long, what they learn, who teaches, who pays and how results are checked. Rules and rights set the entitlement, and money and people decide whether it becomes a classroom where a child learns to read. Each year of schooling pays about 9% on average, yet schooling is not the same as learning.

The World Bank's 2018 report found that in rural India in 2016 only half of grade 5 students could read a grade 2 text. Learning profiles are flat, so gaps start early and widen. Families and markets alone under-provide education, and each failure points to a tool: **money, data, subsidies or law**.

diagram.caption: the four questions the course keeps asking

key_terms.meaning: Extra earnings from one more year of schooling, net of cost.
What each grade adds to what a child can do.
Poor families cannot borrow against a child's future earnings.
An educated person benefits neighbours and voters.
Both Centre and states share the task of school education.

worked_example.title: Read the enrolment edges
worked_example.setup: ASER 2024: 98.1% of rural children aged 6-14 are enrolled. Among 15-16 year olds, 7.9% were not enrolled in 2024 and 13.1% in 2018.
steps: Children aged 6-14 not enrolled: 100 − 98.1 = 1.9%.
The fall in non-enrolment at 15-16: 13.1 − 7.9 = 5.2 percentage points.
Access for 6-14 is largely answered, and the older group is improving.
So the open questions are learning, equity and money.
worked_example.answer: About 1.9% of 6-14 year olds are not enrolled, and non-enrolment at 15-16 fell 5.2 points. Learning is the binding constraint.

mistakes: Treating enrolment as proof of learning. The 2018 report calls this the learning crisis.
Adding school years without fixing the learning profile. It adds cost and little learning.
Using one tool for every market failure. Money, data, subsidies and law fit different failures.

recall.q: What is the average private return to one more year of schooling?
recall.a: About 9% a year, from 1,120 estimates in 139 countries.

recall.q: What is the central message of the World Development Report 2018?
recall.a: Schooling is not the same as learning.

recall.q: What are the four questions the course asks?
recall.a: Access, learning, equity and money.

recall.q: What share of rural children aged 6-14 were enrolled in 2024?
Match credit constraints to their tool.
recall.a: Money.

sections.title: The constitution and the RTE Act
sections.big_idea: The 86th Amendment turned a directive into a **fundamental right** for ages 6 to 14, and the RTE Act gave it content.
in_plain_words: Education began in the Directive Principles, which no court could enforce under Article 37. Mohini Jain (1992) and Unni Krishnan (1993) read a right into Article 21. The 86th Amendment of 2002 inserted Article 21A for ages 6 to 14, kept early childhood as a directive in Article 45, and made education a parental duty in Article 51A(k). It came into force with the RTE Act on 1 April 2010.

The Act's sections turn into plain claims: a free neighbourhood place (s3), no capitation (s13), no corporal punishment (s17), a School Management Committee (s21) and a 25% quota in private schools (s12). **Section 16 changed in 2019** to allow exams in classes 5 and 8. The Schedule sets inputs and says little about outcomes. The courts keep deciding who the Act binds.

key_terms.meaning: Fundamental right to free, compulsory education for ages 6 to 14.
A guide to governance that courts cannot enforce.
Subjects on which Parliament and states may both legislate.
A payment demanded for admission, barred by s13(1).
School Management Committee under s21.

worked_example.title: Which provision, which claim?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a parent of a seven-year-old brings three problems to an NGO desk.
steps: The school demands an entrance interview: s13(1) bars screening, so cite it.
A teacher beats the child: s17(1) bars physical punishment and mental harassment.
The family is in a notified group and wants a private seat: s12(1)(c), the 25% entry quota.
Timing check: the Act was in force 1 April 2010 and the amendment was assented in 2002, so 2010 − 2002 = 8 years.
worked_example.answer: Cite s13(1), s17(1) and s12(1)(c). Article 21A took eight years from the 2002 amendment to come into force.

mistakes: Assuming early childhood is a right. Article 45 is a directive, so NEP's pre-school push rests on schemes.
Judging a school by its Schedule inputs. A school can meet every norm and leave children unable to read.
Assuming one detention rule applies everywhere. Detention is now a state choice.

recall.q: When did Article 21A and the RTE Act come into force?
recall.a: 1 April 2010.

recall.q: Which entry places education on the Concurrent List, and from when?
recall.a: Entry 25 of List III, from 3 January 1977 under the 42nd Amendment.

recall.q: What does s12(1)(c) require?
recall.a: Unaided schools admit at least 25% of the entry class from weaker sections and disadvantaged groups.

recall.q: What did the 2019 amendment change?
recall.a: It substituted section 16: exams in classes 5 and 8, extra instruction and re-exam within two months; no expulsion.

recall.q: What did Pramati (2014) decide?
recall.a: Five judges exempted all minority schools, aided and unaided, from the RTE Act.

sections.title: From Kothari to NEP 2020
sections.big_idea: Sixty years of policy name the **same 6% of GDP target**, and NEP 2020 is a policy that binds only through other instruments.
in_plain_words: The Kothari Commission (1964-66) proposed a 10+2+3 structure, a common school system and spending of 6% of GDP by 1985-86. NPE 1968 adopted much of it, NPE 1986 added Operation Blackboard and an equity focus, and schemes moved the money: DPEP, SSA from 2001, and Samagra Shiksha from 2018. None of the early policies carried a statutory right.

NEP 2020 replaces 10+2 with 5+3+3+4 for ages 3 to 18 and sets targets such as 100% GER by 2030 and universal FLN, now 2026-27. The Cabinet approved it and Parliament did not pass it. **Ask which document turns "NEP requires" into a rule**, and whether your state has adopted it, since education is on the Concurrent List.

key_terms.meaning: 1964-66 commission; its targets reappear in later policies.
1986 scheme to equip primary schools.
2018 scheme merging SSA, RMSA and teacher education.
NEP structure of four stages covering ages 3 to 18.
Hindi, English and the regional language.

worked_example.title: How far from 6% of GDP?
worked_example.setup: Public spending on education as a share of GDP: 2.9% when Kothari reported, 4.43% in 2017-18 and 4.1% in 2022-23. The target is 6%.
steps: Gap at Kothari's report: 6 − 2.9 = 3.1 percentage points.
Gap in 2017-18: 6 − 4.43 = 1.57 percentage points.
Gap in 2022-23: 6 − 4.1 = 1.9 percentage points.
The 2022-23 figure is lower than the 2017-18 one, though the two come from different sources.
worked_example.answer: The gap was 3.1, 1.57 and 1.9 points. The target has been named for sixty years and not met.

mistakes: Calling NEP 2020 a law. It is a Cabinet-approved policy that binds through statutes, rules and schemes.
Quoting NEP's 2025 FLN date as current. NIPUN Bharat set 2026-27.
Comparing spending shares across sources without checking the year and the definition.

recall.q: What were the Kothari Commission's dates?
recall.a: Formed 14 July 1964; report submitted 29 June 1966.

recall.q: How do the Centre and states share Samagra Shiksha?
recall.a: 60:40 in most states and 90:10 in Himalayan and north-eastern states.

recall.q: What are the four stages of 5+3+3+4?
recall.a: Foundational (3-8), preparatory (8-11), middle (11-14), secondary (14-18).

recall.q: What is NEP's higher education GER target?
When was NEP 2020 approved?
recall.a: 29 July 2020, by the Union Cabinet.

sections.title: Access versus learning: the data
sections.big_idea: Enrolment is near universal, so **use the right survey for the right question**: ASER for foundations, PARAKH for competencies, UDISE+ for counts.
in_plain_words: ASER 2024 finds 98.1% of rural children aged 6-14 enrolled, and UDISE+ counts 14,66,682 schools in 2025-26. Primary enrolment is falling with birth rates, while secondary is rising. Dropout climbs from 1.8% in the preparatory stage to 7.0% in secondary, and adolescents leave mainly to supplement household income.

Learning is low. In 2024 more than three in four government school Std III children could not read a Std II text, while arithmetic is at its highest in a decade from a low base. PARAKH shows scores falling with each stage. ASER and PARAKH differ in method on purpose, so **never compare their numbers directly**.

left.title: ASER 2024
items: Share of children at each level

key_terms.meaning: The Ministry's census of schools, with individual student records.
Gross enrolment ratio: all enrolled at a level over official-age population.
Net enrolment ratio: only children of the right age.
National Assessment Centre in NCERT, running the survey.
Household survey of learning run by Pratham and partners.

worked_example.title: Count the school system's change
worked_example.setup: UDISE+ totals: schools 14,71,473 in 2024-25 and 14,66,682 in 2025-26; government schools 10,13,322 and 10,05,245; private unaided 3,39,583 and 3,41,689.
steps: Total fall in schools: 14,71,473 − 14,66,682 = 4,791.
Government schools fell by 10,13,322 − 10,05,245 = 8,077.
Private unaided schools rose by 3,41,689 − 3,39,583 = 2,106.
Falling primary enrolment means more schools with few children.
worked_example.answer: Total schools fell by 4,791, government schools by 8,077, and private unaided schools rose by 2,106.

mistakes: Joining UDISE+ series across the 2022-23 method break.
Reading the ASER-PARAKH difference as one survey being wrong.
Citing a GER without checking the population projection behind it.

recall.q: How many children did ASER 2024 reach?
recall.a: 649,491 in 17,997 villages across 605 rural districts.

recall.q: What are the primary GER figures for 2024-25 and 2025-26?
What are the main reasons given for not attending at age 14-18?
recall.a: Supplementing household income (44%) and domestic chores (28%); distance is 1%.

recall.q: How many students did PARAKH 2024 test?
recall.a: 21,15,022 in Grades 3, 6 and 9.

recall.q: What share of rural Std III children could subtract in ASER 2024?

sections.title: Paying for school
sections.big_idea: States pay most of the cost, the Centre funds schemes with matching rules, and **allocation is only half the story**.
in_plain_words: Every policy since 1966 names 6% of GDP. PRS puts Centre plus states at 4.1% in 2022-23. The Ministry of Education's 2026-27 budget is Rs 1,39,289 crore, of which school education is 60%. A government school draws on the state budget for salaries, Samagra Shiksha at 60:40, PM POSHAN for midday meals and PM SHRI for model schools.

A budget line shows intent. By February 2025 the school department had spent about 59% of its allocation, and teacher training spending fell from Rs 599 crore to Rs 96 crore. Families pay too: a private school costs about ten times a government school. **Inputs alone rarely raise learning**, so ask how the next rupee is used.

key_terms.meaning: Integrated Centre-state scheme for pre-school to class 12.
Midday meal scheme, pre-primary to Grade 8.
Scheme of about 14,500 model schools.
Central money that a state must match to draw.
GEEAP label for inputs alone that do not raise learning.

worked_example.title: Check the Ministry's budget
worked_example.setup: 2026-27 BE: school education Rs 83,562 crore; higher education Rs 55,727 crore; total Rs 1,39,289 crore. 2025-26 RE total: Rs 1,21,949 crore.
steps: Add the heads: 83,562 + 55,727 = 1,39,289 crore.
Rise over the revised estimate: 1,39,289 − 1,21,949 = 17,340 crore.
worked_example.answer: The heads add to the total, school education is 60%, and the budget is up about 14% on the revised estimate.

mistakes: Reading a budget line as money delivered. Release and spending decide delivery.
Assuming free education is free. Families pay fees and costs even in government schools.
Funding inputs alone. GEEAP lists textbooks, buildings, grants and extra teachers alone as bad buys.

recall.q: What was Centre plus state education spending as a share of GDP in 2022-23?
recall.a: 4.1%, per PRS.

recall.q: What is the Ministry of Education's 2026-27 allocation?
recall.a: Rs 1,39,289 crore.

recall.q: How much of its allocation had the school department spent by February 2025?
recall.a: About 59%.

recall.q: How does the deck describe the cost of a private school relative to government?
recall.a: About ten times.

recall.q: What did the absence study estimate for monitoring against hiring?
recall.a: Better monitoring could be over ten times more cost effective than hiring more teachers.

sections.title: Teachers
sections.big_idea: Teachers are the biggest spending decision, and the evidence says **absence falls where someone checks** and incentives work at modest cost.
in_plain_words: India has more than one crore teachers, 54.9% of them women, and national pupil-teacher ratios look comfortable. Distribution is the problem: nearly 10 lakh posts were vacant in 2024-25, one lakh schools have one teacher, and 52% of pre-primary teachers are professionally unqualified. NEP promised time-bound filling of vacancies.

Absence was 25% in 2003 and 23.6% a decade later. Monitoring went with lower absence. Two experiments showed incentives work: a camera-and-pay scheme cut absence from 42% to 22%, and bonuses in Andhra Pradesh raised scores. Balsakhi tutors helped weaker children. **Treat tutors as a complement**, since they do not replace trained teachers.

diagram.caption: four gaps behind the national average

key_terms.meaning: Pupil-teacher ratio.
A school with one teacher for several grades.
Teacher Eligibility Test, held binding by a 2025 judgment.
Samagra Shiksha's in-service teacher training.
A community tutor in Pratham's programme.

worked_example.title: Read the absence figures
worked_example.setup: Kremer et al. (2005): 25% absence across India, 15% in Maharashtra, 42% in Jharkhand. Duflo, Hanna and Ryan: 42% absence in comparison schools, 22% with cameras. Muralidharan et al.: 23.6%.
steps: State spread in 2003: 42 − 15 = 27 percentage points.
Effect of the camera scheme on absence: 42 − 22 = 20 points.
Share of teachers present at the 2017 visits: 100 − 23.6 = 76.4%.
The camera scheme also raised test scores by 0.17 SD after one year.
worked_example.answer: States differed by 27 points, cameras cut absence by 20 points, and about 76.4% of teachers were present in the later survey.

mistakes: Quoting a national pupil-teacher ratio as proof of adequacy. The problem lies in distribution.
Treating absence as a moral failure. It falls where someone checks.
Comparing vacancy counts across states without noting that states set sanctioned posts.

recall.q: How many teachers did UDISE+ 2025-26 record?
What did Kremer et al. find for absence in 2003?
recall.a: 25%, from 15% in Maharashtra to 42% in Jharkhand.

recall.q: What did Duflo, Hanna and Ryan find?
recall.a: Absence fell from 42% to 22% and scores rose 0.17 SD after one year.

recall.q: What did the Supreme Court hold on the TET on 1 September 2025?
recall.a: It binds teachers recruited before the RTE Act; those with more than five years to retire must pass within two years.

recall.q: What is GEEAP's rating of community-hired staff?
recall.a: Promising, with limited evidence on cost-effectiveness at scale.

sections.title: Private schools and section 12(1)(c)
sections.big_idea: Private unaided schools now teach about four in ten children, so **selection bias** and admission rules matter more than raw gaps.
in_plain_words: UDISE+ 2025-26 shows government schools below half of Grades I-XII enrolment, with private unaided at about 38%. Parents say they choose private schools for quality, proximity and English. The raw 59.3% against 44.8% reading gap in Std V mixes school effect and family selection. The Andhra Pradesh voucher lottery found no score gap at lower cost.

Section 12(1)(c) reserves 25% of entry seats, filled by lottery or portal, with the state reimbursing the lower of its own per-child cost and the fee. Sixteen years on, Dinesh Biwaji Ashtikar says rules are needed or the provision is a dead letter. States have four levers, and **information has the clearest evidence**: report cards raised scores 0.11 SD in Pakistan.

nodes.label: State reimburses
nodes.sub: lower of cost and fee, s12(2)

key_terms.meaning: Reserves at least 25% of entry class for disadvantaged children.
A group difference caused by who joins the group.
What the school itself contributes to learning.
Published school test results given to parents.
Minimum conditions before a school can operate.

worked_example.title: Count the reserved seats
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a private unaided school has an entry class of 80 children.
steps: Section 12(1)(c) reserves at least 25% of the entry class.
Reserved seats: 80 × 25 ÷ 100 = 20.
The school declares the 20 seats before applications open.
The state reimburses the lower of its own per-child expenditure and the school's actual fee.
worked_example.answer: Twenty of the 80 seats are reserved, allotted by lottery or portal, with no test or interview.

mistakes: Quoting a private-government score gap as the school's effect. It includes selection.
Using an online-only portal for 12(1)(c). Parents may lack digital literacy.
Assuming the voucher result settles equity. The study does not.

recall.q: What share of Grades I-XII enrolment is in private unaided schools?
What did the Andhra Pradesh voucher lottery find?
recall.a: No gap in Telugu and maths scores after two and four years, at under a third of the cost per student.

recall.q: What does s13(1) bar?
recall.a: Capitation fees and screening procedures for the child or parents.

recall.q: What did report cards do in Pakistan?
recall.a: Raised test scores 0.11 SD, cut private fees 17%, raised enrolment 4.5%.

recall.q: Name two of the four levers to regulate private schools.
recall.a: Any two of: recognition norms, fee regulation, seat mandates, information.

sections.title: Accountability and assessment
sections.big_idea: Accountability needs **information, incentives and capacity** together, and a reform that adds only paperwork changes nothing.
in_plain_words: A system answers for learning when someone knows how children are doing, someone cares, and someone can change what happens. Information without capacity leaves a head teacher able only to file the report. Incentives without information push schools to improve the attendance record. The loop closes with feedback, the next measurement.

National assessment moved from NAS to PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan. School management committees exist on paper under s21 but need information and authority. Report cards help parents. A management reform in 1,774 schools changed no outcomes, and **officials reported more paperwork**. Boards are being asked to lower the stakes, and every number needs its year and source.

key_terms.meaning: Standard-setting national assessment centre in NCERT.
Body of parents, teachers and local members under s21.
Published results that tell parents what children know.
A board exam with attempts to cut the cost of one bad day.
A change that makes one year incomparable with the next.

worked_example.title: Read the NAS table
worked_example.setup: NAS average scores out of 100, 2017 to 2021: Grade 3 language 67 to 62; Grade 5 maths 53 to 44; Grade 10 language 36 to 43.
steps: Grade 3 language fell: 67 − 62 = 5 points.
Grade 5 maths fell: 53 − 44 = 9 points.
Grade 10 language rose: 43 − 36 = 7 points.
The period spans pandemic closures, so avoid a single trend claim.
worked_example.answer: Grade 3 language fell 5, Grade 5 maths fell 9, and Grade 10 language rose 7. Read each cell, with its dates.

mistakes: Counting a committee on paper as accountability. It satisfies s21 and may change nothing.
Judging a reform by compliance measures. Assessments were done and nothing changed.
Joining series across a method break, such as UDISE+ before and after 2022-23.

recall.q: What are the three ingredients of accountability?
recall.a: Someone knows how children are doing, someone cares, and someone can change what happens.

recall.q: What is PARAKH's origin in NEP?
recall.a: NEP para 4.41 proposed it as a national assessment centre.

recall.q: What did Muralidharan and Singh find?
recall.a: A school management programme in 1,774 schools had no impact on school functioning or student outcomes.

recall.q: What does NEP para 4.36 propose for board exams?
recall.a: Lower the stakes; up to two attempts in a school year.

recall.q: Why does the 1 March 2027 Census matter?
recall.a: It will reset the population denominators behind GER and NER.

sections.title: What works: the evidence
sections.big_idea: Information, structured pedagogy and teaching at the right level are **great buys**, and pilots must survive government delivery.
in_plain_words: GEEAP's 2023 report sorted interventions into great buys, good buys, promising, expensive and bad buys. TaRL groups children by level and has worked at scale in two versions. Balsakhi tutors and software raised scores while running, and Mindspark gave 0.37 SD in maths. Structured pedagogy bundles lesson plans, materials and support. Early years and girls' stipends add good and promising options.

Fade-out is common: the balsakhi gain fell from 0.28 SD to about 0.10 SD a year after. Pilots run by NGOs may not hold when governments run them. **Ask who delivered the pilot**, what it cost per SD gained, whether it changes incentives, whether gains lasted and whether it worked in more than one place.

key_terms.meaning: Global panel ranking education interventions on cost-effectiveness.
Teaching at the Right Level, grouping by what children can do.
Adaptive software that serves content at the child's level.
Bangladesh's stipend for girls in secondary school.
Gains shrinking after a programme ends.

worked_example.title: How much gain faded?
worked_example.setup: Balsakhi remedial tutoring raised average scores 0.28 SD. A year after the programmes ended, 0.10 SD remained for targeted children.
steps: Computer-assisted maths started higher at 0.47 SD.
Plan to continue the programme or change the regular classroom.
worked_example.answer: 0.18 SD of the gain faded and about 36% remained after a year.

mistakes: Treating a pilot result as policy. Banerjee et al. show proof-of-concept results may fail at government scale.
Calling hardware a programme. Hardware alone is a bad buy.
Citing GEEAP without noting that panel members include researchers whose studies it rates.

recall.q: Name the three great buys.
recall.a: Information on benefits, costs and quality; structured pedagogy; teaching by learning level.

recall.q: What did Mindspark lottery winners gain after 4.5 months?
recall.a: 0.37 SD in maths and 0.23 SD in Hindi.

recall.q: What conditions did Bangladesh's FSSAP set?
recall.a: 75% attendance, at least 45% in class tests, unmarried until completing secondary school.

recall.q: What are the five scaling questions?
recall.a: Who delivered, cost per SD, incentives or tasks, did gains last, worked in more than one place.

recall.q: What does GEEAP rate quality pre-primary?
recall.a: A good buy.

sections.title: Neighbours and higher education
sections.big_idea: Budgets and constitutions differ across South Asia, yet **the size of a budget does not settle results**, as Pakistan and Bangladesh show.
in_plain_words: India's constitution guarantees ages 6 to 14, Pakistan's ages 5 to 16, Nepal's free education to the secondary level and a mother-tongue right, and Bangladesh's Article 17 commits the state to free and compulsory education. None of the five reaches 6% of GDP, and only India is above 4%. The WDI table uses one source so definitions match, but data years differ.

Pakistan has 26.2 million children out of school and 65% in Balochistan. Bangladesh reached girls with targeted stipends on near 2% of GDP. Sri Lanka's free education since 1945 gives 92.7% literacy and a fiscal squeeze. In India, higher education has about four crore students and a GER of 28%, and the VBSA Bill would **replace UGC, AICTE and NCTE** with one regulator.

key_terms.meaning: Free, compulsory education for ages five to sixteen.
Free basic and secondary education; mother-tongue right.
Higher education enrolment over the relevant age population.
All India Survey on Higher Education.
2025 Bill creating a single higher education regulator.

worked_example.title: Same budget, different result
worked_example.setup: WDI: Pakistan spends 1.95% of GDP (2023) and Bangladesh 2.03% (2024). Primary completion: Pakistan 74.1% and Bangladesh 94.3% (2024).
steps: Spending difference: 2.03 − 1.95 = 0.08 percentage points of GDP.
Primary completion difference: 94.3 − 74.1 = 20.2 points.
So almost the same budget share sits beside a 20-point completion gap.
Budget size alone does not settle results.
worked_example.answer: A 0.08-point spending difference sits beside a 20.2-point primary completion gap.

mistakes: Comparing the learning poverty figures as if they shared a year. They run from 2015 to 2022.
Mixing WDI's tertiary GER of 34.4% with AISHE's 28%. The definitions differ.
Treating the VBSA Bill as law. It has not passed.

recall.q: Which Pakistani article covers ages five to sixteen?
recall.a: Article 25A, inserted by the 18th Amendment in 2010.

recall.q: What does Nepal's Article 31 add that India's 21A lacks?
recall.a: Free education to secondary level, and a community right to mother-tongue education.

recall.q: What is Sri Lanka's adult literacy?
What does the VBSA Bill replace?
recall.a: The UGC, AICTE and NCTE.

recall.q: What is India's higher education GER in 2021-22?
recall.a: 28% per AISHE; Tamil Nadu 47%, Bihar 17%.

sections.title: A practitioner's toolkit
sections.big_idea: Start with ten diagnostic questions, match each problem to the evidence, and **choose the data source built for the question**.
in_plain_words: The ten questions run from enrolment to cost per SD of learning. If you can answer only the first, you are designing an access programme. The decision table pairs diagnoses with responses and traps: TaRL for non-readers, monitoring for absence, report cards for uninformed parents, stipends for girls leaving after Grade 8, trained staff for weak pre-school, and seat publication for unused 12(1)(c) places.

The illustrative block plan tests every child, groups by level, trains teachers and retests. Pair each question with its data source, and when sources disagree check sample, year and method. Work with government through annual work plans and SMCs. For children's data, the DPDP Act applies from 13 May 2027, and a placement test is a decision, so **the research exemption may not apply**.

diagram.caption: match the instrument to the decision

key_terms.meaning: Ten questions asked before designing a programme.
Cost divided by the change in share reading.
State council for educational research and training.
The party that decides how personal data is processed.
DPDP s17(2)(b), which excludes decisions about a person.

worked_example.title: Cost per additional reader
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a block has 6,000 children in Grades 3 to 5; roughly two-thirds cannot read a Grade 2 text. After the programme 1,000 more children can read it, and the programme costs Rs 12,00,000.
steps: Children who cannot read at baseline: 6,000 × 2 ÷ 3 = 4,000.
Children who can read at baseline: 6,000 − 4,000 = 2,000.
Readers after the programme: 2,000 + 1,000 = 3,000.
Cost per additional reader: 12,00,000 ÷ 1,000 = 1,200 rupees.
worked_example.answer: 4,000 could not read at baseline, and the programme cost Rs 1,200 per additional reader. All figures are invented.

mistakes: Using UDISE+ to judge learning, or ASER to count schools. Each source answers a different question.
Assuming the research exemption covers a placement test. Grouping a child is a decision about that child.
Designing around the pilot's NGO. Keep the intervention cheap enough for the state to run.

recall.q: What does the first diagnostic question ask?
recall.a: Are children enrolled? (UDISE+, ASER)

recall.q: Which source answers why adolescents are out of school?
recall.a: PLFS and NSO education surveys.

recall.q: What are the four steps of the block plan?
recall.a: Test, group, train, retest at 50 days and at year end.

recall.q: From when does DPDP section 9 apply?
What does section 9(1) require?
recall.a: Verifiable consent of the parent before processing a child's personal data.

sections.title: Open debates and where next
sections.big_idea: Six debates are unsettled and decided state by state, so **quote every figure with its year** and re-check dates before you cite them.
in_plain_words: The debates cover detention in classes 5 and 8, mother-tongue instruction, school consolidation, private school growth, a single higher education regulator and contract teachers. Each has evidence on two sides. Know both arguments before taking a position, and note that practice differs by state.

Policy moves through survey releases, budgets, court orders and bills. As of October 2026 the pending items are ASER 2026, UDISE+ 2026-27, the end of NIPUN Bharat's target year, Census 2027, the Pramati reference, the 27 October 2026 hearing and the VBSA Bill. **Dates move and court matters are adjourned**, so re-check each. The eight ideas summarise the deck.

items: Detention is now a state choice

key_terms.meaning: A larger bench to decide on RTE and minority schools.
Reference date 1 March 2027; resets denominators.
A teacher hired on a fixed term, with lower pay.
Merging small schools into larger ones.
Sorting children into schools by family background.

worked_example.title: How long has 6% been the target?
worked_example.setup: Every policy since 1966 names 6% of GDP. The deck is current as of October 2026, and spending was 4.1% in 2022-23.
steps: Years since the target was first named: 2026 − 1966 = 60.
Gap in the latest figure: 6 − 4.1 = 1.9 percentage points.
Name the year with each figure: 4.1% is for 2022-23.
Re-check the next test, Union Budget 2027-28.
worked_example.answer: The target is sixty years old and the latest figure is 1.9 points short. Quote 4.1% with its year, 2022-23.

mistakes: Treating a pending case as decided. Check the latest order before citing.
Quoting an old figure without its year. Most will change within two years.
Taking a side without knowing the other side's evidence.

recall.q: Name three of the six open debates.
recall.a: Any three of: detention, mother tongue, consolidation, private school growth, single regulator, contract teachers.

recall.q: What is the Census 2027 reference date?
recall.a: 1 March 2027.

recall.q: What does the hearing on 27 October 2026 concern?
recall.a: Dinesh Biwaji Ashtikar, on 12(1)(c) rules.

recall.q: What share of students do private schools teach?
What is the end slide's advice?
recall.a: Count the children, then count what they learn.

notes.2: Use the agenda as a map. Sections 2 and 3 give the law and its history, section 4 the data, sections 5 to 7 money, teachers and private schools, sections 8 and 9 accountability and evidence, section 10 neighbours and higher education, and section 11 the tools.
notes.4: Education policy covers who goes to school, for how long, what they are taught, who teaches, who pays and how results are checked. Hold two halves in mind: rules and rights set the entitlement, and money and people decide whether it becomes a classroom where a child learns.
notes.5: Remember 9% a year as the average private return to one more year of schooling, pooled from 1,120 estimates in 139 countries, with higher returns for women. The slide's own warning matters: returns are an average across years and show nothing about whether a particular year taught anything.
notes.6: Keep one line from the World Development Report 2018: schooling is not the same as learning. In rural India in 2016 only half of grade 5 students could fluently read a grade 2 text. The report calls this a moral crisis because it worsens inequality for disadvantaged youth.
notes.7: A flat learning profile means each extra year adds little skill. In Delhi in 2015 the average grade 6 student did maths at a grade 3 level, and even grade 9 had reached less than grade 5. Adding years without fixing the profile adds cost and little learning.
notes.8: Match each market failure to its tool: credit constraints to money, information gaps to data, spillovers to subsidies, rights to law. The state need not run every school, yet each reason explains why public money and rules are involved. Use the South Asian example in the last column.
notes.9: Use the four questions as a checklist for any scheme, budget line or evaluation: access, learning, equity, money. ASER 2024 finds 98.1% of rural children aged 6 to 14 enrolled, so access is largely answered. The other three are open, and the course spends its time there.
notes.11: Follow the sequence from directive to right: Directive Principles in 1950, Mohini Jain in 1992, Unni Krishnan in 1993, the 86th Amendment of 2002 and force on 1 April 2010. Article 37 meant no court could enforce a directive. Since 2002 a parent or SMC can go to court for the child.
notes.12: Learn the three-way split. Article 21A makes education for ages 6 to 14 a right enforceable against the State. Article 45 leaves early childhood as a directive. Article 51A(k) puts a duty on parents. That is why NEP's pre-school push rests on schemes with no justiciable right behind it.
notes.13: Education sits on the Concurrent List, entry 25, since the 42nd Amendment took effect on 3 January 1977. The Centre sets higher education standards, but states run most schools and pay most salaries. So a national policy like NEP needs each state to adopt it in rules, budgets and recruitment.
notes.14: Treat the table as seven sections to cite. Section 3(1) gives the entitlement, 12(1)(c) the 25% seats, 13(1) bans capitation and screening, 17(1) bars physical punishment, 21 creates the SMC, 24(1) sets teacher duties, and 25 with the Schedule sets norms. Quote the section number in any complaint.
notes.15: Use this list to turn the Act into claims a family can make. Each claim carries its section, which is what a complaint, an RTI request or a petition needs. Note the last paragraph: officials sometimes cite the parent's duty under Article 51A(k) to deflect the child's right.
notes.16: The Schedule sets inputs an inspector can count: two teachers for up to 60 children, 200 working days and 800 hours in Classes I-V, 220 days and 1,000 hours in VI-VIII. Reasonable in 2009, they say nothing about learning. A school can meet every norm and still leave children unable to read.
notes.17: Section 16 has two regimes. The original barred holding back any child until elementary education ended. The 2019 amendment sets exams in classes 5 and 8, extra instruction and a re-exam within two months, and lets governments allow holding back. Expulsion stays barred. Check your state's rules.
notes.18: Read the six cases as a story. Mohini Jain and Unni Krishnan found the right, the 2012 Rajasthan case upheld the 25% quota, Pramati exempted minority schools, and the two recent cases are pending or ordering rules. Check the latest order, as the source note advises, before citing.
notes.20: The Kothari Commission is the most cited document in Indian education policy. Remember three of its proposals: a 10+2+3 structure, a common school system, and raising spending from 2.9% of GDP to 6% by 1985-86. The 6% figure returns in 1968, 1986, 1992 and 2020.
notes.21: NPE 1968 turned Kothari into national policy but gave no statutory right, because education was then a state subject. Four commitments matter: compulsory education to age 14, the three-language formula, equal opportunity and 6% of national income. The three-language formula is still contested.
notes.22: NPE 1986 added a focus on women, SC and ST, Operation Blackboard and IGNOU, and the 1992 Programme of Action revised it. Like 1968 it had no statutory right behind it. NEP 2020 says the unfinished agenda of NPE 1986/92 is dealt with in its own text.
notes.23: Follow the money. DPEP at 85:15, then SSA from 2001, RMSA for secondary, and the 2018 merger into Samagra Shiksha. The Centre and states now share Samagra Shiksha 60:40 in most states and 90:10 in Himalayan and north-eastern states. The 2026-27 allocation is Rs 42,100 crore.
notes.24: Use the table as a one-page timeline and notice its shape. Early rows are documents about access. From 2019 the rows are laws and measures: the RTE amendment, NEP 2020, NIPUN Bharat and PARAKH. Learn the legal dates: 1976, 2002, 2010 and 2019.
notes.25: Learn 5+3+3+4 as ages: foundational 3-8, preparatory 8-11, middle 11-14, secondary 14-18. The change brings three years of pre-school or anganwadi into the school system for the first time. Light textbooks start in the preparatory stage. The medium of instruction is the home language wherever possible.
notes.26: Treat NEP's numbers as benchmarks: 100% GER by 2030, higher education GER of 50% by 2035, 6% of GDP at the earliest, and universal FLN by 2025, now 2026-27 in NIPUN Bharat. Several dates have passed, so you can judge delivery. The 5 crore figure measures the gap at the start.
notes.27: NEP is a policy approved by the Cabinet. It is no Act of Parliament and does not amend the RTE Act. Each element binds only through a statute, rules, a scheme guideline, a board regulation or a state order. When someone says "NEP requires", **ask which document makes it a rule**.
notes.29: Read 98.1% as enrolment largely solved for ages 6 to 14. Then look at the edges: 7.9% of 15-16 year olds not enrolled, and girls not enrolled above 10% in Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan. The 2022 jump in government enrolment came in the pandemic and has partly reversed.
notes.30: UDISE+ is the census of schools. It has collected individual student records since 2022-23, so earlier years do not compare. Read the two columns: total schools, government schools, enrolment, single-teacher and zero-enrolment schools fell, while teachers and private unaided schools rose.
notes.31: GER can exceed 100 because it counts everyone enrolled at a level against the official-age population, while NER counts only children of the right age. Primary GER fell from 90.9 to 89.4 as secondary rose. A.C. Mehta links the primary fall to falling births, so expect smaller schools.
notes.32: The dropout rate climbs with stage: 1.8% preparatory, 3.6% middle, 7.0% secondary. For ages 14-18, supplementing household income (44%) and domestic chores (28%) lead the reasons, and distance is 1%. That points to cash transfers, flexible schooling and skilling more than new buildings.
notes.33: Government school reading has recovered past its pre-pandemic level, and that is real. Keep the level in view: in 2024 more than three in four government school children in Std III still could not read a Std II text. Compare the Std V gap, 59.3% in private against 44.8% in government, with care.
notes.34: Arithmetic is at its highest in a decade, from a low base. Std III subtraction rose to 33.7% (28.2% in 2018) and Std V division to 30.7%. Std VIII barely moved, at 45.8% against 44.1%, so more than half of children about to finish elementary school cannot divide.
notes.35: PARAKH tested 21,15,022 students in Grades 3, 6 and 9 on 4 December 2024, and the chart shows average scores falling at each stage. Look at the school-type gap too: Grade 9 state government averages of 48 in language and 33 in maths against 69 and 48 in central government schools.
notes.36: Do not put ASER and PARAKH side by side as if they measured the same thing. ASER tests households in rural districts one-on-one and reports shares at each level. PARAKH tests in school on written items and reports average scores. Use ASER for foundations and PARAKH for curriculum-linked competencies.
notes.38: Every policy since 1966 names 6% of GDP. Kothari started from 2.9%, NEP cites 4.43% for 2017-18, and PRS puts Centre plus states at 4.1% in 2022-23. Note the slide's caution: a percentage of GDP is blunt, because GDP growth and falling child numbers change what it buys per pupil.
notes.39: Read the Ministry's budget by head: school education Rs 83,562 crore and higher education Rs 55,727 crore, a total of Rs 1,39,289 crore for 2026-27, 14% above the 2025-26 revised estimate. Samagra Shiksha, PM POSHAN and PM SHRI are the school lines to watch. All figures are in Rs crore.
notes.40: The Union budget is only part of public spending because states pay most teacher salaries. Within the Union's share, Samagra Shiksha, the midday meal and central higher education stand out. PRS puts education at about 2.4% to 2.6% of the Union budget, and WDI at 14.2% of all government spending.
notes.41: Trace a government school's money: the state budget for salaries, Samagra Shiksha at 60:40 (90:10 in Himalayan and north-eastern states), PM POSHAN for meals and PM SHRI for model schools. Matching grants mean a state that cannot find its 40% leaves central money unspent.
notes.42: A budget line shows intent, and release and spending decide delivery. By February 2025 only about 59% had been spent, NIPUN Bharat spent Rs 5,007 crore of Rs 7,178 crore approved (70%), and teacher training spending fell from Rs 599 crore to Rs 96 crore. A March rush buys goods and events.
notes.43: Free education to 14 still costs families. A private school costs about ten times a government school, and average annual cost per government student is Rs 2,863. 27% of government students pay course fees across all levels, while in Grades 1 to 8 about 8% pay Rs 229 a year. Private enrolment kept rising.
notes.44: GEEAP lists funding additional inputs alone as a bad buy. Teacher absence of 23.6% costs $1.5 billion a year in unauthorised absence, and better monitoring could be over ten times more cost effective than hiring more teachers. The argument is about the next rupee: where inputs exist, use decides learning.
notes.46: India has more than one crore teachers, 1,02,73,020 in 2025-26, and 54.9% are women. National pupil-teacher ratios look comfortable against the RTE ceiling of 40, at 10:1 in the foundational stage and 21:1 in secondary. The problem is distribution, with higher secondary ratios of 47:1 in Jharkhand.
notes.47: NEP promised to fill vacancies in a time-bound manner, yet nearly 10 lakh teaching posts were vacant in 2024-25. Learn the five reasons on the slide. Vacancy counts depend on sanctioned posts, which states set themselves, so compare states with care.
notes.48: Single-teacher schools fell from 1,18,190 to 1,00,843 over four years, and zero-enrolment schools from 10,294 to 5,663 after a peak of 12,954. When the one teacher is absent, the school is closed. Merging schools frees teachers but lengthens journeys for the youngest children.
notes.49: The 2003 snapshot is the reference figure for teacher absence: 25% on unannounced visits, from 15% in Maharashtra to 42% in Jharkhand. Learn the contrast. Inspection, better infrastructure and a paved road went with lower absence, while higher pay, local recruitment and parent associations made no difference.
notes.50: Absence fell only a little, to 23.6%, while pupil-teacher ratios improved, and hiring more teachers was associated with higher absence. More frequent monitoring went with lower absence. Remember the caveat: this is correlational panel evidence, and the next slide turns to experiments.
notes.51: Two experiments show incentives work at modest cost. A camera-and-pay scheme cut absence from 42% to 22% and raised scores 0.17 SD. Andhra Pradesh bonuses averaging 3% of pay raised maths 0.28 SD and language 0.16 SD after two years, with gains in subjects without incentives too.
notes.52: Section 23 requires minimum qualifications, yet 52% of pre-primary teachers and 10 to 12% at other levels are professionally unqualified. Qualification is no guarantee of competence, but an untrained teacher of four-year-olds is a direct risk to the foundational stage. NISHTHA had reached 43% of targeted teachers.
notes.53: Balsakhi tutors were young women from the community with far less training, and average test scores rose 0.28 SD, with 0.10 SD left a year after for targeted children. Gains were largest for the weakest. GEEAP rates community staff promising with limited evidence, so treat tutors as a complement to teachers.
notes.55: Government schools' share of Grades I-XII enrolment has slipped below half. Private unaided schools gained about 25 lakh students while total enrolment fell. The 2024-25 shares were 50.83% government and 36.80% private unaided. In rural areas the picture differs: ASER finds 66.8% of rural 6-14 year olds in government schools.
notes.56: Parents in private schools cited unsatisfactory public quality (34%), proximity (27%) and English medium (17%). These are signals a parent can see, while learning levels are hard to observe. That information gap is why report cards and published results can change school markets.
notes.57: Do not read the 59.3% against 44.8% gap as what private schools add. It mixes the school's contribution with the selection of families who pay fees. To isolate value added you need a design that compares similar children, such as a lottery. The next slide describes one.
notes.58: The Andhra Pradesh voucher lottery let researchers compare winners and losers. There was no gap in Telugu and maths scores after two and four years, at under a third of the cost per student, with no spillover harm. The study does not settle equity or segregation, so state that limit.
notes.59: Learn the four-step flow for 12(1)(c): the state notifies groups, the school declares seats, a lottery or portal allots them, and the state reimburses under s12(2) at the lower of its own per-child cost and the school's fee. Section 13(1) bars testing or interviewing, so schools cannot screen for these seats.
notes.60: In Dinesh Biwaji Ashtikar the Court said that without enforceable rules the object of Article 21A and section 12(1)(c) would be a dead letter. Use the list as an audit of local barriers: digital-only portals, languages, hidden seat counts, refusals without reasons. Check the latest order before relying on it.
notes.61: States have four levers for private schools, each with a risk: recognition norms can close low-fee schools, fee caps can bring hidden charges, seat mandates fail on late reimbursement, and information can narrow teaching. Information has the clearest evidence: report cards in Pakistan raised scores 0.11 SD and cut fees 17%.
notes.63: Accountability needs three things at once: someone who knows how children are doing, someone who cares, and someone able to change what happens. Test any system against the chain of information, incentives, capacity and feedback. A head teacher told her school is weak, with no authority to act, can only file the report.
notes.64: NAS became PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan, and the table gives averages out of 100 for 2017 and 2021. Scores fell in grades 3, 5 and 8 in both subjects across the pandemic years. Grade 10 language rose from 36 to 43, so read each cell and avoid a single trend claim.
notes.65: Section 21 requires an SMC, but an SMC on paper satisfies the Act and may change nothing. Schools with parent associations had no lower teacher absence, and GEEAP rates community management promising with limited evidence. Committees work better with information parents can use, authority over some money and a channel to escalate.
notes.66: GEEAP's highest category includes information on the benefits, costs and quality of education. In Pakistan, villages randomly given report cards saw test scores rise 0.11 SD and private fees fall 17%, and enrolment rose 4.5%. ASER's citizen-led testing applies the idea nationally with a number anyone can understand.
notes.67: A large management reform in 1,774 schools made assessments, ratings and improvement plans, yet changed no incentives and had no impact on outcomes. Officials reported more paperwork, and the programme looked successful on compliance measures. Ask of any reform whether it changes incentives or only adds tasks.
notes.68: NEP para 4.36 keeps Grade 10 and 12 boards and asks for lower stakes: up to two attempts, a main sitting and one for improvement. Note the trade-off on the slide: Grades 5 and 8 exams can now lead to detention, so younger children face higher stakes. Check the board's current scheme.
notes.69: Cite the year and source of every number, and do not join series across a method break. UDISE+ is self-reported by schools and, since 2022-23, holds individual records, so it does not compare with 2021-22. The Census with reference date 1 March 2027 will reset the denominators behind GER and NER.
notes.71: Learn the GEEAP ladder from the top: great buys (information, structured pedagogy, teaching by learning level), good buys, promising with limited evidence, effective but relatively expensive, and bad buys. Bad buys are hardware alone and additional inputs alone. The panel reviewed more than 550 evaluations.
notes.72: TaRL has four steps: assess, group, teach, reassess. Children are grouped by level for part of the day regardless of grade. Banerjee and colleagues describe trials that took it from proof of concept to government scale, where some designs failed and two versions raised learning at scale.
notes.73: Balsakhi gave two results: community tutors raised average scores 0.28 SD and computer-assisted maths raised scores 0.47 SD. Both worked while running and helped the weakest most, but only 0.10 SD remained a year after. Plan for fade-out by continuing the programme or changing the regular classroom.
notes.74: Mindspark adapts each question to the level the child has actually reached, often several grades below her class. Lottery winners gained 0.37 SD in maths and 0.23 SD in Hindi in 4.5 months. Absolute gains were similar for all, so relative gains were larger for weaker students. GEEAP rates it promising.
notes.75: Structured pedagogy bundles lesson plans, materials and ongoing teacher support, and each part alone does less. NIPUN Bharat applies the idea nationally, with 2026-27 as its target year and Ministry replies since December 2025 saying the end of Grade 2. Vidya Pravesh is the three-month readiness module.
notes.76: Gaps open before school. GEEAP rates parent-directed stimulation (0 to 36 months) and quality pre-primary as good buys. ASER finds 83.4% of 4-year-olds in a pre-primary institution, and PRS reports 52% of pre-primary teachers unqualified, so expanding pre-school without trained teachers risks pushing formal lessons onto four-year-olds.
notes.77: Bangladesh's FSSAP paid a stipend and tuition subsidy to rural girls who attended 75% of school days, scored at least 45% and stayed unmarried. Girls' secondary enrolment grew 13% a year against 2.5% for boys. GEEAP lists targeting girls as promising and merit scholarships as a good buy.
notes.78: Use the five questions before scaling anything: who delivered the pilot, what it cost per SD gained, whether it changes incentives or only adds tasks, whether gains lasted, and whether it worked in more than one place. Balsakhi fell from 0.28 SD to about 0.10 SD, a warning about fade.
notes.80: Government spending on education as a share of GDP comes from WDI, with a different latest year for each country, so read small differences with care. Only India is above 4%, none reaches the 6% India has targeted since 1966, Nepal has fallen from 4.43% in 2021, and Sri Lanka fell to 1.2% in 2022.
notes.81: Read the table by indicator, and mind the years. India spends 14.2% of government expenditure on education, has a tertiary GER of 34.4% and learning poverty of 56.1% on 2017 data. Primary completion above 100 reflects over-age completers. Use learning poverty only for orders of magnitude.
notes.82: Pakistan's Article 25A covers ages five to sixteen, wider than India's 6 to 14, so it reaches secondary school. Yet 26.2 million children were out of school in 2021-22, and Balochistan is at 65%. The share fell while the number rose because the school-age population grew faster.
notes.83: Bangladesh reached girls with demand-side incentives on a low budget, near 2% of GDP. Compare it with Pakistan: similar spending (2.03% against 1.95%) but primary completion of 94.3% against 74.1%. The size of the budget does not settle results on its own. Learning poverty is a separate question at 51.2%.
notes.84: Nepal's Article 31 goes further than India's 21A, with free education to the secondary level and a community right to mother-tongue education. Spending fell to 3.69% of GDP in 2024 from 4.43% in 2021. Compare how Nepal wrote secondary schooling as a right while India wrote the 100% GER target as a goal.
notes.85: Sri Lanka introduced free education on 1 October 1945 under Kannangara, and adult literacy is 92.7%, the highest of the five. It also shows a fiscal squeeze: education spending fell to 1.2% of GDP in 2022 and is 7.2% of government expenditure. Early universal provision produced lasting gains.
notes.86: Higher education has about four crore students in 1,395 universities, with a GER of 28% in 2021-22 against a NEP target of 50% by 2035. State gaps are wide: 47% in Tamil Nadu and 41% in Kerala against 17% in Bihar. Do not mix WDI's 34.4% with AISHE's series.
notes.87: NEP proposed a single HECI with four verticals. The 2025 VBSA Bill would replace UGC, AICTE and NCTE with one regulator. It went to a Joint Parliamentary Committee on 16 December 2025 and has not passed as of October 2026. Check for a later report or vote before citing the status.
notes.89: Use the ten questions at the start of any programme design, district plan or funding proposal. Each maps to a section and to a source you can open. If you can answer only the first question, you are designing an access programme, and most systems now need learning programmes.
notes.90: Read each row as diagnosis, evidence-backed response and trap. Children cannot read: TaRL and structured pedagogy, with follow-up beyond a one-off camp. Teacher absence: monitoring with consequences, because forms nobody acts on achieve nothing. Parents cannot judge schools: report cards with tests broad enough to resist teaching to the test.
notes.91: Work the illustrative block in four steps: test, group, train, retest at 50 days and at year end. Measure the share reading a Grade 2 text, and find cost per additional reader by dividing cost by the change in the share reading. All numbers on the slide are invented.
notes.92: Pair each question with the instrument built for it: UDISE+ for counts, ASER for reading and arithmetic, PARAKH for curriculum scores, PLFS and NSO surveys for why adolescents are out of school, the Union budget and PRS for spending, AISHE for higher education. When sources disagree, check sample, year and method first.
notes.93: Partnerships work best when they fit the system's calendar and legal hooks. Learn the entry points: Samagra Shiksha work plans, training calendars, SCERTs and SMCs, and the hooks of sections 12(1)(c), 17 and 24. Present results by school and block, and keep the intervention cheap enough for the state to run.
notes.94: A child is anyone under eighteen. From 13 May 2027, section 9 requires verifiable parental consent and bars processing likely to harm a child's well-being. A test used to place a child in a learning group is a decision about that child, so do not assume the section 17(2)(b) research exemption covers programme data.
notes.96: Treat the six debates as open. Detention: effort against pushing children out. Mother tongue: faster reading against parents' wish for English. Consolidation, private growth, a single regulator and contract teachers each have two sides. Know both arguments, since each is decided state by state as much as nationally.
notes.97: These are the pending events as of October 2026: ASER 2026, UDISE+ 2026-27, NIPUN Bharat's target year, Census 2027, the Pramati reference, the hearing on 27 October 2026, the VBSA Bill and the next budget. Re-check each before you cite it, since dates move and court matters are often adjourned.
notes.98: Use the eight ideas as revision. If you keep three: enrolment is near universal for ages 6 to 14 and learning is the binding constraint, education is on the Concurrent List so states decide much of what NEP becomes, and pilots must survive government delivery. Quote each figure with its year.
notes.99: Choose your next course by thread. Foundational Literacy & Numeracy 101 for classrooms, Public Finance & Budgeting 101 for the state, Impact Evaluation 101 and Cost Effectiveness 101 for evidence, and Item Response Theory 101 for how PARAKH puts different test booklets on one scale.
